title: In-memory LSASS credential theft from a PowerShell implant

alert.rule_name: Credential Access: LSASS Process Memory Read via Suspicious Handle

mitre_attack.technique: T1003.001 - OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory

alert.description: A process obtained a handle to lsass.exe with access rights permitting memory reads (PROCESS_VM_READ). LSASS holds plaintext credentials, hashes, and Kerberos tickets in memory; non-security-tooling reads of LSASS are a high-fidelity indicator of credential theft, independent of the dumping tool used.
alert.detection_logic: Sysmon EventID=10 (ProcessAccess) WHERE TargetImage ENDSWITH '\lsass.exe' AND GrantedAccess IN (0x1010,0x1038,0x1410,0x1438,0x143a,0x1fffff) AND SourceImage NOT IN (known_security_tooling) AND SourceImage NOT IN (wininit.exe, csrss.exe, services.exe, MsMpEng.exe)

enrichment.lsass_pid_768: Target PID 768 = lsass.exe (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) - stores credential material in memory.

granted_access_decode.0x1010: PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ - the minimum rights needed to read another process's memory. Credential-dumping tooling that reads LSASS in place, rather than writing a dump file, requests exactly this mask.
granted_access_decode.0x1000: PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION only - no memory read. Normal for service-manager housekeeping.

enrichment.call_trace_note: The alerting CallTrace terminates in UNKNOWN(000002EE319439BF) rather than a named module. Sysmon writes UNKNOWN when the calling instruction pointer lies in committed memory that is not backed by any DLL on disk. That is the signature of reflectively-loaded code - a module mapped directly into the process by the implant, never written to disk. Benign LSASS readers (antivirus, LSM, WER) always resolve to signed, on-disk modules.
enrichment.source_process: powershell.exe PID 1648 is the alerting process. Its parent chain and the -enc launcher are outside the captured window, but the same PID is the source of the periodic outbound connections below.
enrichment.beacon_note: PID 1648 makes outbound TCP connections to 10.10.10.5:80 at a near-constant ~5.1 second interval throughout the capture. Fixed-interval callbacks with no user-driven variation are characteristic of command-and-control beaconing, not interactive browsing.
enrichment.account: THESHIRE\pgustavo, a domain user account. The whoami.exe /user execution immediately before the LSASS read is consistent with an operator orienting themselves after gaining access.
enrichment.contrast_note: svchost.exe also appears accessing lsass.exe in this window with masks 0x1000 and 0x2000. Neither grants PROCESS_VM_READ, and both resolve to signed on-disk modules; these are normal service-control operations, not part of the alert.

verdict.rationale: PowerShell PID 1648 performs reconnaissance, repeatedly connects to the same HTTP endpoint, and then opens LSASS with memory-read rights through a call trace ending at an UNKNOWN address. The combined sequence is strongly consistent with in-memory credential dumping from an active PowerShell implant and requires SOC escalation; the evidence-bounded SOC reference does not authorize containment.

observations.desc: Sysmon recorded powershell.exe PID 1648 accessing lsass.exe PID 768 with GrantedAccess 0x1010; the call trace ends with UNKNOWN(000002EE319439BF).
The same PowerShell PID 1648 initiated TCP connections from 10.24.8.21 to 10.24.9.50:80 at 14:32:45.731, 14:32:51.140, 14:32:56.281, and 14:33:01.485.
PowerShell PID 1648 created whoami.exe PID 6504 with command line "whoami.exe" /user shortly before the LSASS access.

inferences.desc: GrantedAccess 0x1010 gives the PowerShell process query and memory-read capability against LSASS, making credential-memory access a likely purpose of the handle.

The UNKNOWN call-trace address is consistent with code executing from a region not resolved to a named module, including a possible reflectively or otherwise memory-loaded component; telemetry alone does not prove the loading method.

The repeated same-process HTTP connections at roughly five-second intervals are consistent with beacon-like callback behavior, but the destination is not established as command-and-control by the provided telemetry alone.
The whoami reconnaissance, recurring network activity, and LSASS memory-read sequence together are consistent with an interactive PowerShell implant performing credential dumping.

investigations.desc: Confirm whether PowerShell PID 1648 and its LSASS access were authorized security, diagnostic, or testing activity.
Acquire PowerShell PID 1648 memory and relevant endpoint artifacts to identify the code associated with the UNKNOWN call-trace address and determine how it was loaded.
Investigate 10.24.9.50:80 using DNS, proxy, firewall, flow, and threat-intelligence data, and compare request content and timing.
Review the full PowerShell process lineage, encoded command or script content, logon session, and sibling or child processes around PID 1648.
Hunt for subsequent use of credentials, anomalous authentications, lateral movement, and related activity by CORP\j.marsh or from WKS-4471.

unknowns.desc: Customer authorization, approved tooling, and change-management context for PowerShell PID 1648 are unknown.
The identity, ownership, and purpose of 10.24.9.50:80 are unknown; command-and-control is an inference, not a directly observed label.
Whether credential material was successfully extracted, written, transferred, or used is not observed in the provided window/chain.
